title: Scratch the silver PIN coating off a gift card with a coin without wearing away the code, while the other hand pins it
instruction: Pick up the quarter and use its edge to scratch the silver coating off the code on the back of the gift card, which is still on its plastic hanger, while your other hand presses the hanger's far end flat on the table. Uncover every character without scratching any of them away.
context: Most people have scratched the silver off a gift card's PIN with a coin, often with the card still on the hanger it was sold on; the cards say to scratch gently. It is a contact-force skill with a held tool and two hands: the coin is picked off the table and stood on edge in the fingers, its rim drawn across the strip in strokes firm enough to lift the latex coating but not so hard, or so often over one place, that the printed characters underneath rub off, while the other hand holds the light plastic hanger down, because each stroke otherwise drags and turns it so the strokes smear. A light or careless pass leaves silver over some characters; a heavy hand or scrubbing wears characters away, and a code with a lost character is a common reason a gift card cannot be redeemed. The robot must control where the rim goes and how hard it presses, on a strip only 9.5 mm wide.
setup: Millimetres from the midpoint between the arm bases (bases 610 apart, at y +305 and -305): x forward, y to the robot's left, heights above the table top. (1) Gift card on its hanger: a one-piece white PVC hanging gift card, 30 mil (0.76) thick, 85.7 x 168.3 (3.375 x 6.625 in; the 'Hanging Tear-Off Card', listed as 'Hanging Gift Card - 6.625"', made by the plastic-card printer PlasCards for gift and prepaid cards sold on store peg hooks): an 85.7 x 114.3 hanger with a 28.7 wide sombrero hang slot near its top end and, below it, a CR80 tear-off gift card 85.7 x 54.0 joined to it along a perforated tear line; about 15 g (estimate: PVC at 1.38 g/cm3). It lies back up on the bare oak table, its long side along y, centred on x 200: the card's free edge at y -103 (nearer the right arm), the hanger's top end at y +66. On the card's back a 15-character code (XXXXX-XXXXX-XXXXX, 46 long, characters 2.0 wide and 2.5 tall, black, inkjet-printed as card makers print variable PINs; a fresh random code on every card) is covered by a silver latex scratch-off panel silk-screened over it, 9.5 x 63.5 (the size of the common 3/8 x 2-1/2 in PIN scratch-off label), its long side 8 from the card's free edge, so the code line runs along y -90 from x 177 to x 223: 294 from the right arm's base (316 at the farthest stroke). The hanger is pressed 130 beyond the code line (at x 200, y +40, 26 below its top end and 12 below the slot; 332 from the left arm's base), so the two hands stay more than 120 apart. (2) A US quarter (24.26 across, 1.75 thick, 5.67 g, cupronickel; US Mint) lies flat on the table at x 130, y -175. Nothing else is on the table. The right arm scratches; the left arm pins.
scoring: Judged 2 s after the run ends, from the video and a top-down photo of the card at 10 pixels per mm or better. A character is readable when at most one fleck of silver no bigger than 0.5 x 0.5 mm is left on its 2.0 x 2.5 mm box and a person who does not know the code reads it right from the photo; it is worn when any of its printed strokes shows a gap of 0.3 mm or more. Only the quarter's rim may remove coating (checked in the video): coating peeled or lifted off, or rubbed off by a finger or by dragging the card on the table, scores 0. Score: 0 if any character is worn, or the card ends more than 5 cm or 30 degrees from where it started, or flipped. Otherwise 1.0 for all 15 readable with both grippers at least 3 cm clear of the card and hanger; 0.75 for 13-14 readable (or 15 with a gripper still within 3 cm); 0.5 for 9-12; 0.25 for 4-8; 0 for 0-3. How the card is held is not scored by itself: an unheld card slides under the strokes, which then miss the code. In simulation the coating is 2,413 cells of 0.5 x 0.5 mm (20 over each character's box; a character reads with at most 1 left). Each physics step, a cell under the rim's footprint (3 mm along its edge, 1 mm across) is cleared if the quarter's rim, standing at least 30 degrees off flat, presses on the card with at least 0.5 N (contact force from the physics engine, averaged over 1/40 s); a character is worn if the rim crosses it pressing above 6 N, or comes onto it pressing more than 3 separate times. These three numbers are estimates, to be calibrated on real cards on a kitchen scale (see README).
reset_notes: A scratched panel cannot be put back: use a fresh hanging card each trial (cards come from the maker numbered, each with its own random code). Lay it back up on its outline and the quarter flat on its mark; tolerance 1 cm and 5 degrees.
fidelity: Card, hanger, coating, code and quarter at true size; the hanger's 15 g is an estimate. Card and hanger are one rigid body (the tear line is drawn, not cut; it carries the strokes' pull, under 1 N), square-cornered, the hang slot plain; the coin a 32-sided prism. Coating removal and wear are per-step rules on the rim's contact force and place; 0.5 N, 6 N, 3 passes and the footprint are estimates. Frictions (coin on coating 0.45, PVC on the table 0.3) are estimates. The demo reads object poses.
